transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alyssa Park (Redwood AE), Jonas Rivera (Redwood SE), Sophie Turner (NovaApps - Head of ML), Arun Patel (CTO), Diego Morales (SRE)

Summary:
Quick walkthrough of Redwood model "playlist" concept (a lightweight curated set of open models + fallbacks), how compatibility matrices map to runtime kernels and quantization, and a short bench plan using NovaApps prompts. Customer wanted clarity on latency/cost tradeoffs, on-prem vs hosted, and security controls. Action items captured below.

Topics covered:
- Model playlist concept and selection heuristics
- Compatibility matrix: kernels, quantization, and hardware mapping
- Bench plan and metrics (p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1M tokens)
- Routing/fallback strategy for graceful degradation
- Security and data residency concerns (VPC/private control plane)

Action items (recap): see metadata fields for owners/dates.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Alyssa Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a 40-ish minute walkthrough of a model playlist flow, and Jonas will jump into the compatibility matrix and bench plan. Sophie, Arun, Diego, thanks for making time.
[00:00:12] Sophie Turner: Yep, thanks. We have about 3 product folks watching but I'm the main contact. Looking forward to seeing concrete bench numbers.
[00:00:20] Jonas Rivera: Quick agenda: why playlist (speed up shortlist), how we map models to kernels and quant profiles, then bench plan and next steps.
[00:00:30] Arun Patel: Important for us is predictable latency - we have customer-facing chat with 150ms p95 target. Also cost matters but SLA > cost.
[00:00:38] Diego Morales: And we need VPC/private deployment options, data can't leave our VPC for some of the workloads.
[00:00:45] Alyssa Park: Great notes. The playlist is basically a curated ordered set — a primary model, a lighter quantized variant, and a fallback. We surface compatibility in the console; it ties to kernel availability and quant support.
[00:00:58] Sophie Turner: When you say quantized variant, is that like int8 or lower? What's the quality hit?
[00:01:06] Jonas Rivera: Good question. We recommend a two-tier quant strategy. For 8-bit (int8) you typically see very small quality drift on synthesis tasks but for instruction-heavy prompts there can be reg regressions; we flag those with our eval sets. For extreme latency sensitive routes we have nf4/quant profiles that reduce memory and improve throughput.
[00:01:28] Arun Patel: Do you have public numbers comparing quant vs fp16 across different sequence lengths?
[00:01:33] Jonas Rivera: We do, and we'll include tailored plots in the bench run. Quick example: on A100-equivalent infra, for a 512-token typical request, int8 throughput was ~1.7x fp16, p95 latency reduced ~25% in our internal tests, cost per 1M tokens drops materially. But again, depends on model and prompt type.
[00:01:55] Sophie Turner: Okay that helps. How do you map models in the playlist to hardware? If we run private, we use our on-prem GPUs, does that change compatibility?
[00:02:07] Jonas Rivera: Yes, compatibility matrix is per-architecture. We map model ops to kernel libraries (our runtime picks the best kernel at serving time). On-prem GPUs that don't support certain fused kernels may fall back to a slightly slower path. That's in the matrix — e.g. some older V100 configs won't hit the same perf as L40s.
[00:02:28] Diego Morales: Any special config for NVLink or shared KV cache when running private?
[00:02:33] Jonas Rivera: For high-throughput workloads we recommend NVLink/fast interconnect and our KV cache configured with IPC (if on same host) to avoid repeated recomputation. We'll put recommended topologies into the deployment guide.
[00:02:47] Alyssa Park: Let's pivot to the console — I'll share my screen — (audio: brief screen share noise) — you'll see the playlist UI which lets you pin order, add model variants, and define fallbacks.
[00:03:10] Alyssa Park: (narrating) Here's a playlist called "support-shortlist" with three entries: 1) a 7B open model tuned for instruction, 2) a quantized 7B int8 variant for burst traffic, 3) a smaller 3B fallback for cost-sensitive flows. You can set routing policy per route: latency-first, cost-first, or region-first.
[00:03:40] Sophie Turner: Can we set a strict SLA enforcement so anything above x ms automatically switches model?
[00:03:46] Jonas Rivera: Yes, the routing policy supports threshold-based fallbacks — you can define p95 latency thresholds and if violated traffic shifts to the next playlist model automatically, with per-route rollout windows.
[00:03:58] Arun Patel: What about function-calling / tooling behavior across variants — is tool calling deterministic across quantized models?
[00:04:06] Jonas Rivera: In general yes, but we've seen edge cases when tokenization differences lead to slightly different parse outputs. We surface structured-output regressions in our evals and you can pin models for routes that require deterministic tool calling.
[00:04:21] Sophie Turner: The compatibility matrix you mentioned — can you show an example mapping to kernels?
[00:04:26] Jonas Rivera: (shares matrix) Here's the table: rows are models, columns are kernel ops and quant formats. Cells indicate fully supported, partial, or fallback. We auto-annotate expected throughput and memory footprint per hardware class.
[00:04:44] Diego Morales: I notice "partial" for one of the ops on our listed GPU, what does partial mean?
[00:04:49] Jonas Rivera: It means we have a slower fallback kernel for that op on that hardware. It will work but throughput might be 20-40% lower. We call that out because customers often want to know the delta up-front.
[00:04:59] Sophie Turner: For the bench, what metrics should we care most about? We have both chat and async summarization use cases.
[00:05:05] Jonas Rivera: For chat, p95 latency and tail tokens/sec matter most, plus quality on a fixed prompt set (we report ROUGE / BLEU / custom evals depending on task). For async batch summarization, tokens/sec and cost per 1M tokens are more important. We'll capture both in the harness.
[00:05:23] Alyssa Park: Quick aside on cost: Redwood Optimize will give suggestions like batch size, prefix caching and quant profile per route — those changes can halve unit costs in some workloads.
[00:05:34] Arun Patel: About caching — if we use prefix caching, does that require keeping any customer data in Redwood? We need to preserve ephemeral policy for PII.
[00:05:42] Jonas Rivera: Cache is encrypted and can be configured to respect retention policies. For strict PII rules you can opt out of persistent caching and use ephemeral in-memory caches per request; we'd document the tradeoffs.
[00:05:55] Sophie Turner: Security — we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs. Do you support SAML and customer-managed KMS?
[00:06:02] Alyssa Park: Yes, SAML SSO and RBAC are supported, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for Private deployments and the console includes audit trails. We'll send the SOC2 report and the security appendix after the call.
[00:06:14] Diego Morales: For Private, how does networking work? Can we run the control plane inside our VPC?
[00:06:20] Jonas Rivera: We offer a private control plane option that can be deployed in your VPC or as an on-prem package. Some teams run the inference plane on-prem and the control plane in a customer-managed cloud VPC; both are supported.
[00:06:32] Sophie Turner: Great. Let's talk bench specifics — timeline and model choices.
[00:06:36] Alyssa Park: We're proposing a 2-week bench sprint: week 1 we baseline 3 models on your prompts (primary, quant variant, small fallback) across hosted and private infra if you want; week 2 we iterate on quant/kv cache and do tuned runs. Expected deliverable: throughput/latency/cost table + qualitative eval notes.
[00:06:55] Arun Patel: If we do private runs, we need to coordinate a small test cluster. Diego will provision.
[00:07:01] Diego Morales: Yep, I can spin up a 4-GPU test box L40-equivalent with NVLink for the run, want SSH access for Redwood?
[00:07:07] Jonas Rivera: SSH for bench harness is easiest; we also support containerized runner. We'll share exact requirements in the bench checklist.
[00:07:15] Sophie Turner: How do you handle model licensing for open models in the playlist? Any compliance checks?
[00:07:21] Alyssa Park: We track model licenses and surface incompatible licenses in the console. For upstream open weights you need to comply with their license; we flag GPL-style incompatibilities.
[00:07:30] Arun Patel: Any notes on drift detection? If we switch quant profiles can we detect regressions automatically?
[00:07:35] Jonas Rivera: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring tied to prompt sets; we can run periodic evaluation and fire regression alerts when a metric deviates beyond a threshold. You can auto-roll-back to pinned models on a failing regression.
[00:07:49] Sophie Turner: That rollback is super important for us.
[00:07:52] Alyssa Park: Noted. Okay, quick demo of bench plan tab — here we upload the prompt set, define model variants, select hardware targets and pick test matrix size (samples x seq len). You can also opt into structured output checks.
[00:08:12] Jonas Rivera: We'll run three canonical tests: latency (single concurrent requests), throughput (sustained concurrent streams), and quality eval (on holdout prompts). We'll produce plots and a short recommendations doc.
[00:08:25] Diego Morales: Any way to replicate our production tokenization exactly? We use a slightly custom tokenizer pipeline.
[00:08:31] Jonas Rivera: You can provide your tokenizer or we can run using your dockerized tokenization step in the bench harness — that gives the most accurate apples-to-apples numbers.
[00:08:42] Sophie Turner: Great. A few logistical Qs: pricing cadence, reserved capacity guarantees, and SLAs for Dedicated?
[00:08:50] Alyssa Park: Pricing: hosted is usage-based; dedicated is committed capacity with lower unit rates and SLA-backed latency/uptime. We'll send a dedicated quote with commit tiers. SLA details and uptime numbers are in the enterprise appendix.
[00:09:05] Arun Patel: What's the expected timeline from bench to pilot? If numbers look good we want a 6-week pilot.
[00:09:10] Alyssa Park: That's feasible — bench (2 weeks) -> pilot kickoff -> 6-week pilot. We can aim to start pilot week of 2026-07-06 if we get prompts and infra access this week.
[00:09:21] Sophie Turner: Perfect. Any blockers from Redwood's side?
[00:09:24] Jonas Rivera: We just need the prompt set, tokenization artifacts and SRE access for private runs. Also, confirm which models you want in the initial playlist.
[00:09:33] Diego Morales: I'll provision the test cluster and drop SSH keys in the shared folder.
[00:09:37] Sophie Turner: I'll upload prompts by Friday and confirm the pilot ROI metrics.
[00:09:42] Alyssa Park: Awesome. Last quick Q: competitors — are there any feature gaps customers usually call out?
[00:09:48] Jonas Rivera: Sometimes teams compare to single-vendor model APIs for simplicity, or to pure self-host infra for total control. Our differentiator is the end-to-end playlist + runtime + optimize tooling to keep ops low while preserving control.
[00:10:02] Arun Patel: Makes sense.
[00:10:04] Alyssa Park: Ok recap — we will: 1) run bench with 3 models on your prompts across hosted and private if you want, 2) share pricing and security docs, 3) schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2026-07-06. Action items in the notes.
[00:10:20] Sophie Turner: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[00:10:24] Diego Morales: Thanks.
[00:10:26] (meeting continues with brief Q&A about token limits, tooling)
[00:30:00] Jonas Rivera: small side conversation — token limits: we suggest truncation policies in the console and streaming to keep latency down.
[00:31:05] Sophie Turner: For longer docs we might prefer chunking + retrieve to avoid hitting token SLOs.
[00:32:12] Alyssa Park: Yup, Redwood has built-in helpers for chunking and reranking in the SDK.
[00:36:40] Arun Patel: One more practical: how does billing break down for pilot infra if we run private?
[00:36:47] Alyssa Park: For private pilot we typically include bench time as a professional services line item and then bill dedicated usage per the committed capacity. We'll detail that in the quote.
[00:37:05] Sophie Turner: Cool. We'll await the bench plan and quote.
[00:37:12] Alyssa Park: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the links: bench checklist, SOC2 appendix, and the pricing sheet.
[00:37:20] (end)
